subject: zenGarden
reasoning:
I'm planning a stylized Japanese garden diorama, around 8 meters across, standing on the ground plane, keeping the part count, color palette, and triangle budget within reasonable limits while using only reliable, well-supported APIs.

My design will combine a raked gravel bed, a small pond with stepping stones, a stone lantern, a cloud-pruned pine tree, a wooden pavilion with a curved roof, bamboo clusters, a tiled garden wall, scattered rocks, and moss patches to create a recognizable garden scene.

I'm planning the layout at roughly 10x8 meters, keeping z as forward depth with the viewer facing +Z, and working out how the ground slab sits at y=0 while respecting the floor-contact tolerance rules.

Now I'm picking out a color palette for the garden elements—moss, gravel, water, stone, wood, roof, pine, bamboo, and sand—and thinking through how to attach parts without a skeleton, using a single root joint at the origin since everything just needs the nearest-joint default.

Writing geometry helpers...

For the raked gravel, I'm planning a thin box near the ground slab's top with a sine-wave paint pattern radiating from a point to simulate rake lines, alternating between two sandy tones.

I'm checking the import path for the paint/stripes helpers, confirming it matches the reference signature from the module.

Now I'm planning moss patches with boxes and cylinders, plus a stepping-stone path using flattened cylinders via the scale option. For the pond, I'm layering a stone rim cylinder around a slightly recessed water disk cylinder to create a sunken pool effect.

Working through the exact vertical placement so the water isn't hidden under the rim — I realize a solid rim cylinder would occlude the water, so I'm switching the rim to a torus shape rotated to lie flat, letting the water disk sit visible in the center, with the ground plane set below both.

Now I'm designing a stone lantern beside the pond, stacking an octagonal base, cylindrical post, lantern box, and small pyramid roof with a finial sphere on top, assigning a warm tan color to the lantern body. For the pine tree, I'm planning a tall trunk with cloud-pruned foliage made from flattened, scaled spheres positioned at staggered heights to get that layered pine silhouette.

For branches I'll use simple rod primitives connecting points along the trunk rather than anything fancier. I'm sketching a bamboo grove with a cluster of thin green cylindrical stalks placed using deterministic sine-based positioning instead of a random generator, to avoid ambiguity around how the rng function behaves. Then I'm outlining a back wall structure with a boxy base and a stacked, slightly offset roof to suggest a tiled slant.

Now I'm planning a small wooden pavilion with a raised deck, corner posts, and a four-sided hip roof built from a low-segment cone rotated 45 degrees to form a pyramid shape, working out the vertical positioning so the roof sits just above the post tops.

I'm then layering in detail elements: scattered stone rocks shaped with scaled icosahedrons, low clipped shrubs, a stepping-stone path from the pond to the pavilion using faceted cylinders, and a red maple tree for a splash of color. I'm also tallying up the material palette across stone, moss, gravel, raked sand paint, water, wood tones, walls, roofing, pine, trunk, and bamboo to keep the scene cohesive.

I'm now working out spatial placement for the garden's main zones: the back wall, pond, raked sand area, bamboo grove, pine and maple trees, stone lantern, and pavilion deck, carefully checking their coordinates and sizes so nothing overlaps.

I'm also figuring out the ground slab dimensions and wall position, then planning stepping stones leading from the pond toward the pavilion, placing the stone lantern near the pond's back edge, and clustering rocks near the pine tree.

I'm checking rock placement against the pond's edge to avoid overlap, repositioning them further out, then adding clipped shrubs near the pavilion front while keeping clear of the deck edge.

Next I'm placing bamboo along the back corner, then building a pine tree with a trunk and layered foliage pads at different heights using flattened spheres in alternating colors. For the sand area, I'm writing a paint function that generates concentric sine-wave rings around a rock island, alternating between two sand tones to create a raked-sand pattern.

I'm positioning the rock itself—an icosahedron scaled unevenly to look like a boulder—and working out its vertical offset so it sits naturally embedded in the sand rather than floating or sinking through it. Then I'm laying out the raked-gravel box and checking it aligns properly with the pavilion deck's edge before moving on to a stone ring around the pond.

I decide to skip a bridge entirely to keep the scene clean, and I'm also skipping pine branch rods to avoid unnecessary complexity. For the maple tree I'm placing a brown trunk cylinder with red foliage spheres positioned near the back wall, making sure the canopy peeks above it, and adding pink dot spheres for azalea blossoms. Now I'm working out the stacked cylinder dimensions for the stone lantern—base, pillar, cap, and body—calculating each piece's vertical position so they sit flush on top of one another.

Writing lantern roof and finial...

Then I move to the pavilion structure, sizing the deck, corner posts, and cone-shaped roof so the eaves properly overhang the posts beneath, checking that the rotated square base of the cone roof aligns correctly with the post positions.

Next I'm laying out stepping stones along a path, then placing nine bamboo stalks with varied height, position jitter, and alternating colors, before starting on a boundary wall.

I work out the sign convention so the front slope tilts down toward the front: front slope gets rotation [12,0,0] centered around y 1.85, back slope gets [-12,0,0], with the ridge meeting roughly at the right height. I decide the exact ridge alignment is approximate enough and move on to setting roof and wall colors.

Now I'm defining a sand paint function that uses a sine pattern based on distance from a point to create a mottled tan/beige texture, and noting pond water could get similar noise treatment but I'll skip that for now. I add a few flat moss patch cylinders scattered near the pond edge and under the pine tree, set the ground slab to a mossy green, and define shrub shapes using squashed spheres with small pink dots for azalea blooms, then start placing the pine foliage as similarly squashed spheres at different heights.

I'm working out the pine tree with layered foliage spheres of decreasing radius and a tapered trunk cylinder sized to stay hidden beneath the canopy, then move to the maple tree with its own tapered trunk and three overlapping red canopy spheres positioned so the bottom stays above ground level and doesn't clip through the nearby wall. I check that the lowest points of all elements rest properly on the ground, and set up a small helper function to simplify placing geometry with position, rotation, and scale options, making sure to add flat shading for a low-poly look.

Now I'm finalizing the build: returning the root node, adding metadata, and writing the complete builder code for the Japanese garden, double-checking that only the actually-used imports (createBuilder, paint) are included and nothing undefined like an unused rng slips through, while keeping the bamboo loop and comments concise.
